package arrays;
import java.util.*;
public class Intersection {

	public static void main(String[] args) {
		// TODO Auto-generated method stub
		Scanner sc=new Scanner(System.in);
		int n=sc.nextInt();
		int a[]=new int[n];
		for(int i=0;i<n;i++) {
			a[i]=sc.nextInt();
		}
		int m=sc.nextInt();
		int b[]=new int[m];
		for(int j=0;j<m;j++) {
			b[j]=sc.nextInt();
		}
		for(int i=0;i<n;i++) {
			boolean d=false;
			for(int j=0;j<i;j++) {
			
				
				if(a[i]==a[j]) {
					d=true;
					break;
				}
			}
			if(d) {
				continue;
			}
			//it skips current iteration
			boolean f=false;
			for(int j=0;j<m;j++) {
				if(a[i]==b[j]) {
					f=true;
					break;
				}
			}
		
		if(f) {
			System.out.print(a[i]+" ");
		}
		}
	}

}
/*# Example Explanation for `j < i` in the Intersection Program

Consider the following array:

```java
a = [5, 2, 5, 3, 2]
```

The loop is:

```java
for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {
    if (a[i] == a[j]) {
        d = true;
        break;
    }
}
```

We use `j < i` because we want to compare the current element only with the elements that come before it.

## When `i = 0`

```java
a[0] = 5
```

There are no previous elements, so no comparison is made.

`5` is not a duplicate.

---

## When `i = 1`

```java
a[1] = 2
```

Compare with previous elements:

```java
j = 0

2 == 5 → false
```

`2` is not a duplicate.

---

## When `i = 2`

```java
a[2] = 5
```

Compare with previous elements:

```java
j = 0

5 == 5 → true
```

A duplicate is found.

```java
d = true;
break;
```

Then:

```java
if (d) {
    continue;
}
```

The second `5` is skipped.

---

## When `i = 3`

```java
a[3] = 3
```

Compare with previous elements:

```java
3 == 5 → false

3 == 2 → false

3 == 5 → false
```

`3` is not a duplicate.

---

## When `i = 4`

```java
a[4] = 2
```

Compare with previous elements:

```java
2 == 5 → false

2 == 2 → true
```

A duplicate is found, so it is skipped.

---

## Why not `j < n`?

If we write:

```java
for (int j = 0; j < n; j++)
```

The program will also compare:

```java
a[i] == a[i]
```

For example:

```java
a[2] == a[2]

5 == 5 → true
```

Every element would be considered a duplicate.

Therefore, `j < i` is used to compare the current element only with the elements before it.
*/
